question: Can our gut verdicts on imaginary cases count as real evidence about right and wrong?
answer: Yes. Ethics tests principles against considered judgments much as science tests theories against observations; John Rawls called the back-and-forth reflective equilibrium. If a theory says a surgeon may kill one patient to save five, the shock is data. Without verdicts on cases, a moral theory would have nothing to answer to.
move: It turns on whether a gut verdict about a made-up case tracks anything real.
ask: Which of my strong moral reactions have I ever tested by changing the details of the case?
counterpoint: Experimental philosophers found that verdicts on imagined cases shift with the order cases are read in. Swain, Alexander and Weinberg showed in 2008 that whether people said a man with a temperature-reading implant knew the temperature depended on what they had read just before. A gauge that drifts with its order is not yet a gauge.
reference: Swain, Alexander & Weinberg, The Instability of Philosophical Intuitions: Running Hot and Cold on Truetemp, Philosophy and Phenomenological Research 76 (1), 2008; Rawls, A Theory of Justice, Harvard University Press, 1971
